items.title: Haul 10% heavier during harvest
bullets: Trucks hauling corn, soybeans, wheat, potatoes, sugar beets, carrots or timber can be up to 10% over normal weight limits.
Applies on state and local highways. Interstates aren't mentioned — check before using them.
The truck's registration has to cover the heavier total weight.
Also eases federal driving-hours (hours-of-service) limits for these hauls.

items.title: Red diesel on the road
items.sub: Federal penalty pause through Dec 31 · Minnesota law unchanged
bullets: The federal government paused its penalties for red (dyed) diesel in road vehicles through the end of 2026 — reports say the federal tax may still be owed later.
Minnesota says its law has NOT changed: no red diesel in road trucks, and the state diesel tax (about 33¢/gal) still applies.
Iowa paused its penalties — rules differ by state.
We'll update this card if Minnesota changes.

items.title: ARC / PLC sign-up for 2026
items.sub: USDA Farm Service Agency · sign every year
bullets: Pick ARC or PLC for each crop and sign the contract at your FSA office.
Marshall County USDA Service Center (FSA and NRCS share the office).

items.title: Red diesel vs. road diesel — the basics
bullets: Red (dyed) diesel has no road tax — it's for off-road farm use: tractors, combines, loaders, generators.
Trucks driven on public roads need clear (taxed) road diesel, unless the law changes (see the Alerts tab).
Keep every delivery ticket — the app's ⛽ Fuel tanks page keeps them for your accountant.

items.title: Driving hours during planting & harvest
bullets: During planting and harvest, drivers hauling farm crops within about 150 air-miles of the farm are generally exempt from federal hours-of-service limits.
Outside that distance or season, the normal limits apply.
This year's governor's order also eases hours limits for harvest hauling.

items.title: Truck weight — what to check
bullets: Registration (license) weight must cover what you actually haul.
Posted bridges and spring load limits still apply, even during harvest relief.
Elevator scale tickets are your proof of weight — keep them with the load.

items.title: NRCS EQIP On-Farm Energy
items.sub: USDA NRCS · year-round sign-up · ranking cutoffs
bullets: Step 1: helps pay for an energy audit (Agricultural Energy Management Plan).
Step 2: cost-share to buy or retrofit equipment — grain dryers are on the list.
Scores on energy saved: bushels dried and points of moisture removed — mostly your corn.
Don't buy or put a deposit down before the contract is signed.

items.title: FSA Farm Storage Facility Loan
items.sub: USDA FSA · up to $500,000 · 15% down · up to 12 years
bullets: Covers grain drying and handling equipment that's essential to your storage — conveyors listed; concrete pits may qualify (ask about the dump pit and leg).
Microloan option up to $50,000 with 5% down.
Must be approved BEFORE any site work or equipment delivery.

items.title: USDA REAP
items.sub: Paused March 31, 2026 until USDA rewrites the rules
bullets: No grants right now — before the pause, most Minnesota REAP grants went to grain dryers.
The loan guarantee still works: ask your bank about a REAP guarantee (up to 75% of project cost).
We'll update this card when grants reopen.

items.title: Electric co-op rebates
items.sub: Fans · motors · variable-speed drives on new handling
bullets: Call the co-op that serves the bin site (Red Lake Electric or PKM).
Most rebates need pre-approval before you buy.

items.title: MN Dept. of Agriculture grants
items.sub: Electric Farm Equipment (last round closed Aug 11) · AGRI programs (usually winter)
bullets: Electric Farm Equipment Grant: $1,500–$150,000, 25% match — electric augers, motors and similar.
We'll post here when the next rounds open.

items.title: Diesel well above last harvest
bullets: Farm groups report diesel costs up about 70% from last harvest; national average was about $6.38/gal in early October.
MN Corn Growers are asking for red diesel on the road and a state fuel-tax break.

items.title: Minnesota diesel tax unchanged
bullets: MN Revenue says the federal red-diesel order doesn't change state law; a change would need the Legislature.
The governor's office says it is still evaluating options on fuel costs.
